utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Having dealt with a lot of housekeeping matters yesterday, we now resume the presentation of the Prosecution's case. Mr. Hannis, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour. Our next witness is Azim Medanovic. There are no protective measures for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Hannis, the Chamber received an 89(F) summary. Are there any objections against that summary, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it then can be read. It was a bit unclear on whether you wanted to use that, but I think from the last messages, I understood that you'll read the 89(F) summary and concentrate on the remaining issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the very first thing that I'm going to be showing the witness is the 89(F) package, which contains both his statements, his 1997 original statement and then a very brief supplement dated 30 January of 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If that could be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the package to be given one number, including the 17th of July, 1997, and the 23rd of September, 1997 statement, and the supplemental information sheet dated the 4th of October.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P309.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Medanovic. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Medanovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll first be examined by Mr. Hannis, counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Hannis, would you please explain to the witness, unless he Knows already, what the 89(F) procedure means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Examined by Mr. Hannis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Medanovic, we're going to start this morning by handing you copies of your prior statements to the ICTY, and as we discussed when we were proofing this matter, I'm going to ask you if you recognise those statements and adopt them for purposes of evidence in this case. If you'll wait just a moment, we'll have you take a look at those. Mr. Medanovic, before coming to court today in preparation for your testimony, did you have an opportunity to read both those statements?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after having done so, were you satisfied that they were true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The statements are true and accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you now at this time confirm them to the Court as your evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those are my statements. That's what I stated, and I stand by what I stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would note, as we're going to go through his statement, that in the English version of the statement there are a number of minor typographical errors, but rather than go through them one at a time as we did on a previous occasion, I think the meaning of those will be obvious. In one place the word ash is used when it's actually referring to the posterior, and one place riffle is used instead of rifle, those kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If they're obvious typos, which do not leave any doubt as to what they stand for, we can be very practical and leave It. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to read now a summary of his statement. If I may do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. This witness describes a mass killing of non-Serb villagers in and around Prhovo, Kljuc municipality, on or about 1 June 1992. The witness was in Prhovo when Serb infantry and APCs came to the village. Villagers were told to come out of their houses or they would be killed. Immediately after surrendering, male villagers were lined up, facing a wall. Some were singled out, beaten, and shot dead. Surviving men were then marched out of the village toward the village of Peci. Six men at the end of the line were told to push a Serb vehicle out of the mud. They failed to do so, and the witness heard shots and deduced that those men were killed. As the Muslim men were being led toward Peci, one of the Serb soldiers was shot. The leader of the soldiers, local Serb Marko Adamovic, then shouted over his megaphone, "I order the following: Kill women and children, burn the village to the ground." He then heard an explosion, screams and cries coming from the village where the women and children had been left. The marching prisoners were moved on and beaten by soldiers. About eight of them fell, and the witness heard screaming and shots. He deduced that those who had fallen were killed. Further on at a road junction, Adamovic beat the prisoners with his rifle but the. Five more could not continue and were killed. After passing the hamlet of Sisarice, prisoners were ordered to strip and beaten again. Three hundred metres further on, the prisoners were ordered to lie down in a meadow. The witness heard shooting and then an order for those who were still alive to stand up. Adamovic said, "There are too many of them." Two more prisoners were told to kneel down and killed with shots in the back. Marching on, the column passed through a Serb village. The soldiers encouraged the Serb villagers to beat the prisoners. The witness begged one of the Serb soldiers to kill him. As night fell, the column stopped outside the PTT building in the village of Peci. The prisoners were given their most severe beating yet. One more man, about 60 years of age, died. Prisoners spent the night lying bound outside on the gravel. The following day, the prisoners were loaded into a van and driven to the elementary school in Kljuc. A policeman, Tode Gajic, told them that the village of Prhovo was supposed to be erased from the map and that they should be happy that they had survived. All but one of the prisoners were then taken by bus to a school gymnasium in Sitnica. The witness remained there for three days and was then taken on a forced walk of 40 to 50 kilometres to Manjaca, where the witness remained confined for over six months. He lost 30 kilogrammes during his detention. Your Honours, this is relevant to paragraphs 16, 17, 19 through 24 and 27, as well as counts 1 through 8 of the indictment, and schedule killing A, number 9.1, and schedule C, detention facilities 1.4, 19.2, and 19.3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll ask you one question, Mr. Hannis, just for scheduling purposes. The time indicated at the bottom of the 89(F) summary, is that the one still valid? Because I saw another one this morning. You thought that you might be finished even until the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to give you an impression, since we started late, we'll split up just the time in two halves, so I expect that we'll have our first break at approximately a quarter past 12.00, something like that, then have a short break, 20 minutes, and then we would then have two times 70 minutes and the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be less than the three hours that were originally estimated for this witness. And he has a commitment tomorrow, Your Honour, so I'm hoping that we will be able to finish him completely today. Otherwise I would request that he be allowed to come back at a different day if we don't finish him today. Because he does have a work commitment tomorrow that would not make it possible for him to be here tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not even in the early hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I believe there's some test with regard to his employment that he has to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's see how far we come, and, Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Adamovic, according to your statement, you were born and raised in Prhovo village in Kljuc municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of Prhovo village?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: All the inhabitants in that place were Muslims, but there was also a Serbian hamlet called Prhovo, but it was about a kilometre or two away from our village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many houses --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In May of 1992, how many houses, approximately, were there in Prhovo?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: There were about 40 houses, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many people in total lived in Prhovo?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I think about 250 or 260 inhabitants lived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, there's a series risk of confusion, since the witness said that at a distance of one kilometre that the village was also called Prhovo. So could we make sure that we're talking about the Prhovo where he lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Medanovic, if you heard the judge, I want to be clear that the 40 houses and the 250 or 260 inhabitants are the Prhovo, the Muslim Prhovo where you lived. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the purely Muslim Prhovo in which I lived, and that's where there were about 40 houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the witness be shown the next exhibit. This is a map, and could it be given the next number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P310.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Medanovic, could you take a look at that map --

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but my name is not Adamovic. My name is Medanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On our transcript, it appears as Mr. Medanovic, but of course I'm fully aware of if you understood it or if it was translated to you by that other name, that that's not something you would like to remain uncorrected. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Medanovic, could you please take a look at the map that's on Your left, on the screen -- on the flat screen to your left.

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at the screen now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could take the pointer, and on that map could you point to the Court where your village of Prhovo was located.

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that map indicates that the villages in blue are Serb and those in green are Muslim. Based on your knowledge of living in that area all your life, does that appear to accurately reflect the Serbian and the Muslim villages and towns in Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. I think it is accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, and does that also show some of the other villages that you talk about in your statement, including Peci, Humici, Plamenice?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see Peci here, Humici over here. I also mentioned Donje Sokolovo. I said that we saw it as we were on our way to Peci on one occasion. Everything is Kljuc to me. This is where we saw Donje Sokolovo from.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, You can set the pointer down. And we won't need the map for a while, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one thing, Mr. Hannis. There is some text on this map as well which is not there in translation. Of course the graphics are, even for this Chamber, understandable, because a lot of well-known words appear. But the other parts, if it's irrelevant, at least the Defence is able to decipher that. But if you say it's of no importance, then ... But as usual, the Chamber would prefer to have of any exhibit an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. For purposes of this witness, I only wanted to show the graphic representation of the villages. We may have additional testimony about other items contained on that map at a later date from other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we also receive an English translation. Ms. Loukas, would you insist, if you think it's really important what's there, then it's indicated by Mr. Hannis that we'll receive evidence on that later and then we'll receive a translation. But for the time being, could we do without that translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then the Chamber will not insist on --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I have the advantage of having Ms. Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I leave it to the parties at this moment. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Medanovic, in May of 1992, what kind of work were you doing when you lived in Prhovo?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I used to have my own private lorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, in paragraph 6, you say that you were "aware of the tense situation in the municipality in April, May 1992." Could you explain to the Court what tense situation you were aware of at that time. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, there was a sort of anarchy in our municipality. Troops would march around the municipality, troops that never used to be there. They carried automatic weapons with them, which was not allowed before. Soldiers weren't allowed to carry automatic weapons around the town with them or go into cafes with such weapons. This wasn't the case a few years ago, a few years earlier. Many of the people's rights had been curtailed. Some people had been dismissed from their workplaces because they were Muslims. A curfew had already been introduced; from 10.00 in the evening onwards, you weren't allowed to go outside. If necessary, you had to inform people of the need to pass through the town. I was aware of this situation. I was aware of the fact that something was being prepared. I was aware of the fact that something was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the soldiers that you described with automatic weapons, do you know what ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally, they were Serbs. None of our people were there. Our troops were elsewhere. I remember soldiers who came home. They had to leave. These soldiers had to leave the army and go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Medanovic, I want to ask you about paragraph 8 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about paragraph 8 of your statement. You talked about a meeting you went to in Pudin Han, and then you returned to the village and the women had already left to go to Hripavci, H-r-i-p-a-v-c-i. Why had they gone to that other village?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably for their own safety. Not probably. That was for sure. Our village was surrounded by a forest. It was an isolated village, surrounded by Serbian villages. But for the safety of women and children, there were a number of Muslim villages there, so they withdrew to the village of Hripavci, in order to be safe. We stayed on in the village that night, or for another two nights, and then a day or two later the women returned to the village in order to live normally again. But they couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in paragraph 9 of your statement that one Suad Hadzic and two other men went to a neighbouring Serb village for advice and information. Do you know why they had gone there and what kind of advice or information they were seeking?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, our situation was very uncertain. That's the sort of situation we were living in and we didn't have any information from the media, from the television or from the radio. We couldn't obtain any accurate information. So we went to see our neighbours, to request assistance, because there were a few houses there and they had spent their entire lives there together. We just wanted to ask for help, ask what we should do. Two or three men went there. I know that Suad Hadzic and two other men went there. I don't know their names. They went there, but they weren't given a warm reception. But nothing happened to them. They returned home safe and sound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mention in paragraph 10 of your statement the three men that they talked to there, Marinko Suknovic, Branko Brankovic, and Stojan Tekic. What was the ethnicity of those men?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that Suad told you that he and the other two men from your village were told that you people in Prhovo should go to Peci to surrender. Did you do that? Did you go to Peci to surrender?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't. That had no logic. Going to Peci would have meant going through a Serbian village and we couldn't know what would happen to us. While passing through Serbian villages without arms, something would probably have happened to us. We couldn't leave the village, because we didn't have any kind of escort. No one could have escorted us to Peci. We didn't do that. We just waited to see what would happen in our village. We remained there alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next day, according to your statement, paragraph 11, for the Court, Serb military arrived in the village and you and some others went to the forest. When you came back, did you find out from the villagers who remained behind, what had happened regarding the soldiers who came to Prhovo?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, those soldiers allegedly came to take over weapons. The weapons we had were surrendered, were handed over, very few of them, and some people in the village were beaten up. This is what I saw when I returned. I saw that people had scars on their faces. I saw that they had been beaten severely. I was in the forest, and I then returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- forward to paragraph 13 in your statement. June 1st, you described the Serbs coming again. Do you know approximately how many there were?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly, there were about a hundred of them. I wasn't able to count them all, of course, because you weren't allowed to look. But I did see a large number of people who had come to the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: They were wearing the uniforms of military policemen, and the military policemen's uniform included white belts and straps and military pistols with white halters. They had automatic weapons, but of course the weapons weren't white. The weapons were black. And they had white bands on their shoulders. That was some kind of insignia too, or way in which they differentiated between each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say when they arrived you and about ten other men were outdoors. What were you doing at the time?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were there discussing what to do at that particular moment, or rather, that same day, I had it in mind to escape. I didn't believe the soldiers that came in, and if they had confiscated the weapons, they weren't about to do anything else but kill us. But the neighbour said that we should stay in the village because if we were to leave, they would kill the women and children, and I remained and surrendered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... armed at that time? 21

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody had anything left. Everybody handed in their weapons and nobody had any weapons with them any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 14, you describe how you were told to come out of your houses or you would be killed, and you were assembled in the village. Where did they gather you or assemble you? And could we --

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: That was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, go ahead. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: That was in the middle of the village. It was across from the shop. There was Abid Osmanovic's house there. And they lined us up against the wall, the men, and then they took out one by one to kill them or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Exhibit 262, which has previously been shown to another witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please wait for the end of the answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you're invited to wait until the answer of the witness is finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Medanovic, do you recognise what that is a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise that. That is Abid Osmanovic's house, afterwards, once it was destroyed. When they brought us there, it was standing, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... building, where were you villagers gathered by the soldiers, or the military police?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: In front of this destroyed house, up against that wall there. Can I have something to point with to show you? This is where we were, along this wall. We were lined up against this wall, in a group, one next to the other. Several lines of us. We were standing there and waiting what was going to happen to us, what the military police was going to decide to do with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement you say there were about 40 of you men. How many women and children were there in addition to the 40 of you?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were women and children, yes. I can't give you a figure, but, roughly, perhaps 80 women and children. Some of them had gone to live abroad. So there might have been a hundred. No, they weren't there. Some of them were hiding in a cellar. But there were that amount of women and children. They were hiding in another cellar in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement that your wife and child and others were hidden in a basement. Were they able to remain hidden throughout the day?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were just there during the time that the command came, the order came from Marko Adamovic, and I quote: "Kill the women and children and set fire to the village and raze it to the ground." And at the same time, that's what happened. That's what the soldiers did. When they did that and accomplished that, they left the village, whereas the people who remained alive, the women and children remaining in the group behind us, started screaming and crying. And then the women who were hidden in the cellars, they came out to see what had happened in the village itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Medanovic, I want to stop you there and back up a little bit before we get to that event. When you 40 men and some women and children were gathered there in paragraph 15 of your statement, you say the Serbs made your release conditional upon the surrender of certain people. What people did they want in exchange for releasing you?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were looking for Hasan Medanovic and Braco Medanovic, because they knew they were in Germany, the two of them, those two men, and they asked us for something we weren't able to deliver for us to be released. That was the condition they made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement you indicate that you told the Serbs that those two men weren't there because they were working in Germany. And you say the Serbs knew that. How did they know that?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that Branko Brankovic, who was just a kilometre and a half away from us, he had worked with Hasan and Braco Medanovic for several months in Germany before the war began and then he went back there. So he knew that the two men were in Germany and I assume some other people knew about that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they were not able to find these two men that they wanted, what did they do?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: They began to take out the men, one by one, out of the line-up, and to kill them. There were a couple of people there, and usually they would say that they weren't there when the weapons were being handed in. They took those out and started killing them, the ones that had fled and taken to the forest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when had the Serbs been there before this day to look for weapons? How long before?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all that took place in the space of two or three days, from, say, the 28th to the 1st, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were not present on that earlier day when they came to search for weapons. How was it that you were not selected out with these other men?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that point, a military policeman did single me out and take me out. But then he found out that he knew me from the town, and then he protected me. And he said -- he didn't let them take me. He said I was there, whereas I wasn't. He said that he saw me there when the weapons were being handed over. So that's how I stayed alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that the man with the nickname Mrki that you mention in your statement?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's the young man who protected me on that particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among those Serb military men in military police uniforms, how many of them were wearing a mask?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but I think there might have been, let's say, 30 per cent of them. That's what I think. I don't know the exact number. Because the people that we didn't know didn't have to wear masks. People who have been from other places, they had no need to wear the mask because nobody would recognise them. Whereas the people that were well-known to us and were from neighbouring villages, they were the ones who wore the masks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 16 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Hannis. Microphone, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 16 of your statement, Mr. Medanovic, you describe a number of villagers who were singled out, beaten, and killed. Approximately how many men did that happen to in the village before you were taken away?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that there were about seven or eight of them. I can't give you an exact number, but I do know that that was roughly the number, seven, eight, maybe nine, not more than that, there in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was happening with the rest of you men and the women and children who were gathered there during this time?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, an order came from Marko Adamovic to the effect that we were to be lined up on the road towards Peci. And once we had lined up - there might have been 35 of us, 35 men. The women had already been separated and the children too to one side - I was standing next to my own father and I'll never forget that. He told me that I should be careful and take care, and I told him to take care too. And then after a little while they told us to start moving out of the village, in a column, one by one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the last time you spoke to your father?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him that day?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: He was killed and he was found in a mass grave later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the 35 of you men were gathered up, you say in your statement that you were marched off toward Peci. Who was the man that appeared to be in charge of these Serb military policemen?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to conclude, Marko Adamovic was the man that everybody contacted and asked and addressed him. The policemen would always address him and they would say Comrade Captain, what are we going to do next and he would issue an order. So I know he was the man that everybody asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Medanovic, if you need at any moment some additional time or just would like to have a moment of rest or a break, then please indicate, ask me. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Medanovic, in your statement, you say you knew Marko Adamovic before this. What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were the soldiers who escorted you 35 men out of the village toward Peci? Were they the same military policemen you've described or was it some other group?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were the same men. They were still the same men. And they took us to Peci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your way out of town or of the village, in paragraph 20, you say: "A Serb soldier was killed." And you say that was probably by a mistake. What leads you to conclude that that was probably by a mistake?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it must have been a mistake, if nobody else had weapons. So who could kill people if you had handed in your weapons the day before and if we were all gathered there in a group? Nobody else could have done the killing but him. And they were playing around with us, in fact. Or perhaps what might have happened, I think they had to justify Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. themselves and then they could use this as justification and say that one of their own men was killed. Or perhaps it was somebody who wasn't obeying orders. That could have been the case too. But it couldn't have been any of us killing the men, because we were all gathered there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Marko Adamovic do or say anything after -- immediately after that Serb soldier, policeman, was shot?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when that happened, when the incident took place with that soldier, I didn't myself see it actually happening. However, Marko Adamovic became very angry. He was very angry with us, and he turned round to the village, although we were about three to five hundred metres away from the village at that point, and he had a megaphone to issue his orders. And I remember well when he said, "I order the following," and I quote: Burn down the village to the ground. Kill all the women and children." And then I had no hope of surviving. Because what could I expect if they were going to kill the women and children? I would probably have been killed too. Those were the thoughts that went through my mind at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Marko Adamovic gave that order over the megaphone, what happened next? What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: That same moment, you could hear some shots in the village. I think there was a bomb or some explosion of some kind. They had thrown something into the mass of people there, the women and children who had remained there in the village. And you could hear the screams of those people who had stayed on there. And afterwards, I heard that a lot of people were killed on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you men moved on from that point, in paragraph 22 of your statement, you say, about another eight men were killed there. Were those bodies also recovered from a mass grave?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Those bodies were recovered. Because ten days later, they had to come up and pick the bodies away from the -- off the road, and then they buried them all into a mass grave. And two or three of our men were present there, two or three Muslims, when those bodies were you brought back to the village. And then they dug a grave in the centre of the village and put all the bodies inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On down the road, in paragraph 23, you indicate you came to a crossroad and saw a man you knew as Milan Dancic. What was his ethnicity and where was he from?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the man's name was Milan Dancic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his ethnicity and where he's from?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: By ethnicity, he was a Serb, and he was from Serbian Prhovo, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he wearing any kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: He was wearing a uniform, but he wasn't wearing the military police uniform like the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind did he have?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: He had an army uniform, the standard type of army uniform, an ordinary one, the kind that every rank-and-file soldier wears.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 24 you mention another approximately five men being killed, and then going on down to the road, where in paragraph 27 you describe those remaining villagers among you lying down and then another round the shooting fired. You say 14 remained alive after that. What did Marko Adamovic say after that round of shooting?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember him saying Those of you who were still alive, get up. But I thought that all of us were still alive, because I was alive. I didn't see who was actually dead. And when I stood up, a lot of people didn't stand, because they were dead. They were lying down on the ground dead. But I didn't see them actually shooting at us. I thought they were shooting up in the air.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of you were remaining at this time of the original 35 or so?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, 14 of us remained, I think. 14, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your statement, you say Marko Adamovic said that was too many. Did he tell his men to do anything about the fact that 14 of you were too many?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was astonished to see so many of them, and he said: "Oh, there are too many of them." And then he said we should line up and then some more killing took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described that the first two men in line were killed one after another and that you were then the first in line. What happened at that point?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that point, when they singled out those two men and shot them with their pistols - yes, they used their pistols to shoot them - I was the third man in line, and then I was the first after the two others had been shot. And I just saw death before my eyes. I saw my own death before my eyes. I didn't see how I was to survive. Because they took one man out, one by one, and they would just lay down on the ground dead. And I saw my own death, if I can put it that way. I began to perspire, because it's very difficult to know when you're going to die. Very difficult. And suddenly one of the policemen turned around and he came towards me. I recognised him. He wasn't wearing a mask. He was actually a colleague of mine. I knew him from the cafe bars. We would drink coffee together from time to time. And I asked him: Is that you? And he said: Yes, it's me. But it was very difficult to recognise them all in these uniforms and they had their hair cut. But I did recognise him. And he said hello and I asked him to protect me. And he said he would protect me. He recognised me. He said he'd keep me safe, he'd protect me, and he told me to stand away, a few metres away from there, in a line. I was the first man there. And he took me to Peci himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the man that you describe in your statement as Sico?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I just know him by his nickname, Sico. I don't know his first and last name, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now you're down to 12 after these two men in front of you have been killed. What happened next? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they told us to line up. I was the first man in the line. And Marko Adamovic said that they should stop and not use any more bullets from their weapons, because they'd be needing it for something else shortly. And we were happy to hear that, that they didn't want to spend any more bullets on us. So we stood in line. I was the first man. I was the one in front and the other 11 were behind me. And we continued along the road to Peci. We were with almost within reach of Peci, a kilometre away from Peci. Although Peci is a large place, so we had to walk another three or four kilometres, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your statement, Mr. Medanovic, in paragraph 29, you say when you arrived in Peci, that some of the local Serbs came out and began beating you and your fellow villagers. Did that include women and children among those who were beating you?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. They would come out of their houses and they'd say Give us one. We want to slaughter him or them. And then they beat the people. The policemen didn't let them take the people. But they were encouraged in beating the people. And they beat us themselves. So they didn't mind the locals beating us up either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, may I just raise a very practical point. Ms. Loukas, I asked Madam Registrar, in view of the witness who said that he would rather return tomorrow and since it was indicated by Mr. Hannis that he might then have to be recalled, I asked Madam Registrar to explore whether there would be any time available this afternoon. But first of all, I'd like to know whether -- how much time you think you would need for cross-examination. Mr. Hannis, is it still your estimate that you could finish until the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- Your Honour, page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm on page 6 of eight pages of notes, so I'm nearly three quarters of the way through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So there's a fair expectation that we could by the next break that you might be finished. Ms. Loukas, do you think that you could cross-examine the witness in the time that would then remain available or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I have no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No doubt about that. Then we'll continue and ask Madam Registrar to discontinue her further investigations on what could be done this afternoon. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mention in paragraph 29 that you actually asked Sico to shoot you at this point. Why did you do that, Mr. Medanovic?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, while I was being beaten along the road by one of them, he made me take my jacket off, and I stripped -- I had to take everything off except my trousers. And he beat me across my back. I asked him to shoot me, but he too said that bullets were very costly and shouldn't be wasted on the likes of me and that I ought to be hung. And that's what I was afraid of, that he would actually hang me. I would rather have died from a bullet wound than be hanged. It's an easier death.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have the next photograph given an exhibit number and show it to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be ....

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P311.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were in Peci were you taken to, Mr. Medanovic? What part of the village?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they took us right here, in front of this building. Perhaps we were five or ten metres away from the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is that building, or what was it at the time?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a shop in that building, a post office, some sort of a centre. I went there very rarely, but I know there was a post office there and a shop. And behind there was another building, a primary school that had three or four classes. But you can't see the building in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that you were beaten at this location. Who was beating you when you were here?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Across the road, behind the forest, there was a Serbian cafe. That's where they came from, reservists came from there. Although Sico told me on the way that we would be handed over to the reserve forces and that they were going to sleep and have a rest. That's where they came from, and they beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that one more of the remaining 12 of you died at this time. Sulejman Medanovic, was he a relative of yours?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He was a relative of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was guarding the remaining 11 of you villagers that evening?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: We were guarded by the reservists. There was someone else there, Obrad Ribic. He was a driver in Kljuc. As I drove a lorry, I knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And paragraph 33 of your statement, you say the next day you were taken to an elementary school in Kljuc. How long were you there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: We stayed there until dusk. We were there for about seven or eight hours in total.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was guarding you at the elementary school?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the reserve police force, or the police, guarded us there. It was difficult for me to see anyone from Peci. When we spent the night there, my eyes were closed and I couldn't see any more. I didn't see anyone any more. Sulejman Medanovic, who remained lying there, he was dead, I didn't see him personally, although we spent half a day there in Peci. But I couldn't open my eyes any more because my head, my entire face, was swollen. And I wasn't able to see for another two or three days. Then I managed to see after having put water on my eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the elementary school, you say in paragraph 33 that a policeman named Tode Gajic came in and spoke with you, that Cazim Medanovic told Mr. Gajic about what had happened in Prhovo. Do you recall roughly, and briefly, what Cazim told Mr. Gajic about that?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do remember what happened very well. Cazim naively started telling this person called Gajic about the incredible things that had happened to us, as if Gajic knew nothing about that. And as he was telling him about what had happened - how people had been killed, how the village had been destroyed, et cetera, et cetera - at the time, Gajic just kept nodding his head and questioned him and coldly observed him, while this person complained to him. And then Gajic reacted by saying that we should no longer exist, that we should be wiped away from the map, and he said other things to this effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that he said Prhovo was supposed to be erased from the map. Did he tell you why?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't say why. All he said was that in their opinion, that village should no longer exist; it should no longer be seen on the map; it should be destroyed. That was what was literally said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 34, Mr. Medanovic, you say that of the 11 of you who had survived, one 16-year-old was released, and the remaining 10 of you were taken to Sitnica school, where you were detained with about 300 other men. Who was guarding you at the Sitnica school?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: We were guarded there by the reserve police force. It was the police. And the reserve police force was also there, because the active -- they were active at the time, the reserve police force was active and they were assisting the other police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise any of the reserve police guarding you at that school?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I had contact with one policeman who used to work in Humici, in a shop. I recognised him. He approached me. He helped me. He gave me a sandwich, because I was really dead-beat and he felt sorry for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally, he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the 300 men that were detained there, what was the ethnicity of those 300?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: The 300 men there -- well, I don't think there were any Croats among them. I think that they were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the ten of you were from Prhovo. Do you know where the other men were from?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the others were from the surrounding villages in the place called Kljuc, for example, Krasulje, Plamenice. We knew some of the people. There were others whom we did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 35 that on the 5th of June you were taken to Manjaca, or that you had to walk to Manjaca. Of the 300 detained at Sitnica school, how many were taken to Manjaca on that day?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: We were all taken there, all 300 of us. That hall remained empty. They took all of us up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who escorted or guarded you on the march to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was the reserve police force. They were armed, and they escorted us up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could the witness next be shown Exhibit 264, which has previously been tendered in this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Medanovic, I believe in preparation for today you had a chance to see this document before, which lists the names of certain men captured or killed in Prhovo. Would you look at number 3 on that list and tell us who that is.

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: That's myself, Azim Medanovic, son of Ahmo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the document it indicates that you had grenades on that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. day. Did you have any grenades?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No weapon of any kind?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the footnote, it lists a number of names of men who are described as having been killed "in fighting with army and police members." First of all, you looked through those names yesterday and you indicated that one of them listed as killed is still alive. Can you tell the Court which one that is.

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I was revolted by this list of people killed. The list here is by Serbs from Kljuc. Where are the children and women who had also been exhumed from the graves? If there was a fight and if that was some sort of resistance, how is it they managed to conceal who the women and children were? But I can tell you who was killed who wasn't in this list. But I'm just wondering why they didn't compile a list of everyone who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand your question, sir. For now, could you tell us which name you recognise as being someone who is still alive?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Medanovic Cazim, Mulanovic Suljeman, Azim Medanovic, we are alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the top of the list, those are people listed as being captured that day, but in the bottom the footnote are the names supposedly killed. Could you just look at the footnote and tell me if there's one in there you know to still be alive.

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I can. Yes. Jusic Amir, son of Latif. He lives in London now. He's alive. He was with us in Manjaca. He was taken after the ten of us had arrived there. He came after our arrival there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I stop you there for a moment. You mentioned that your father was killed on that day. Is his name among the list of those killed?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: No, unfortunately. No. I had a look at the list yesterday, and this also affected me somewhat, seeing that he is not contained in this list. Perhaps there are others who are not included in the list, but I couldn't say who at the moment, because it's very difficult for me to know who is included there and who isn't from that entire place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I see that you're looking at the clock. How much time you would still need? Because if we would have to finish by today, and when I said that the time would be split up in two times 70 minutes, then of course if you had more questions, then of course time might not be sufficient for Ms. Loukas. At the same time, since it's an 89(F) witness, of course the 60 per cent rule certainly would not strictly apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it will take me another 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that causes then a problem. Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know that it necessarily does. I think we could take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If I could have a short conference with Mr. Krajisnik, and the rest of the evidence in chief can continue. Because, as I indicated previously, there is no doubt that cross-examination would be completed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that would mean that we would now have a break until approximately 25 minutes to 1.00. Then, Mr. Hannis, you would have until ten minutes to 1.00, approximately, and then in the remaining 55 minutes, Ms. Loukas, you confirm that you would be finished by a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Without a doubt, Your Honour, and I might indicate in view of the fact that I want to have a short conference with Mr. Krajisnik during the break, can we have a slightly longer break than Your Honour indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then 20 minutes to 1.00, would that do, or a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: A quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for another late start, but it was in an attempt to even be able to deliver the two pending decisions, if possible, this morning, we spend some time on that. Mr. Hannis. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom. Mr. Medanovic, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Medanovic, I just want to ask you a couple more questions about that list. Among the men from Prhovo listed as being killed that day, do you know that indeed those men listed were killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do know, because all these men listed here were found in a mass grave in the middle of the village. They were exhumed and a record was made, or rather, they were registered as having been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Medanovic, were you or any of those men on that list -- the captured men and the men listed as killed -- were any of you involved in fighting or engaged in combat on that day?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no one was involved in the fighting. The fact that we had handed over the weapons a couple of days earlier is proof of the fact. No one opened fire from any sort of weapons. There was no fighting of any kind. When the police entered, they said: Put your hands behind your head and look to the ground. And we didn't react in any way. We didn't open any sort of fire. We lined up immediately and we remained in the position we were in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that document. Now I want to ask you a question about your stay at Manjaca. In paragraph 36 of your statement, you mention that you were not personally interrogated, but some others were. Do you know if any of your fellow Prhovo villagers were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Medanovic Cazim, from Prhovo, was interrogated. He was interrogated by Tode Gajic, from Kljuc. He is the person who interrogated us in the school too. I heard this from him when the police took him to Manjaca. And when he was returned to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us in your statement that you stayed at Manjaca until 16th of December, 1992. During that time, were you ever charged with a crime or taken to court?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No one took me to court, and no one charged me with anything. They just imprisoned me and kept me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the witness be shown the last exhibit, a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please assist us, or rather, assist Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P312.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Medanovic, do you see the photograph on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise where that's taken?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: That's at Manjaca. I even know some of the men in the photograph. They're from the neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which neighbouring village are those men from?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I know these two here, the second in the line, the third person in line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From which side of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the photograph could be put on the ELMO so that whenever the witness points to certain persons, that -- Mr. Medanovic, may I invite you to do any pointing at the ELMO so that we can follow you.

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I know this young man, I know this man. I don't know this one. I know this man here. And there is no one else I know. I do know these three men here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: The second, the third, and the fourth person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe the second, third, and fifth person [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Medanovic, I think you pointed at the second, the third, and then the fifth person. Is that correct? If you look at the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The second person, the third person, and the fifth person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That, then, has been corrected. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you tell us which village they were from?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this -- the second and third men are from the village of Plamenice [Realtime transcript read in error: "Puminica"], which was three or four kilometres from our village, whereas the fifth man is from the village of Krasulje. He was related to a woman in Prhovo and he would often come to my village. I know him personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, Mr. Medanovic, the first village you named came across as Puminica, but you described it as a village as being to you and I think that has a different name. Could you tell us the village those first two were from?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Plamenice. Plamenice is the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm finished with that photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Medanovic, I want to ask you: You tell us in your statement that you were released in December of 1992. In preparing for your testimony today, we came up with a supplemental information sheet regarding two matters that you had not included in your statement. And one of those was: You mentioned that you had to fill out some paperwork before you were allowed to leave Manjaca. Could you tell the Court what that was.

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all I know is that in order to leave Manjaca, we had to sign a document. We were briefly told about this. But we didn't have time to read what we signed, and they didn't allow us to do so. But we had to sign the document in order to leave Manjaca, and everyone was glad to do this. No one was interested in what the document contained. All the detainees were interested in was leaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember anything about what was in that document you had to sign, or what the condition was that you were agreeing to?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would object to leading on this particular aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could have the supplemental information sheet marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is part of the 89(F).

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I don't believe it was included in the 89(F) package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not included. Okay. Perhaps, Mr. Hannis, let's first try -- Do you remember what exactly was in the document you signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't remember what it contained, but I heard from people, and there were many people in Manjaca who had to sign the document, and according to the rumours, it said something to the effect that you were relinquishing your property, that you were leaving the country, and that you would never return; that you were leaving the land and that you would never return. That was a condition that had to be fulfilled in order to leave Manjaca. It stated that you were going to some third country. That is the sort of document that one had to sign. But there was something that had probably been agreed with the Red Cross, and so all the people went to third countries. They left in droves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And didn't you then read that document before you signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't read anything. There wasn't time to read the documents. Thousands of people signed these documents in half an hour. You'd just line up, you will sign the document, and then you would leave, and the next one would turn up to sign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But just for my understanding: When you signed, you had heard those rumours already before or did you hear them later on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that these rumours were heard before, but this didn't mean anything to us. What we were signing didn't mean anything to any of us. The only important thing was to leave. It didn't matter what they were requesting, whether they were requesting a signature. Whatever the request was, people were prepared to sign documents as long as they could leave. We really weren't interested in what we were signing, because we were fighting for our survival. And that is what is the most important thing for people. People want to save their lives, and it doesn't matter what you are signing. It wasn't important for me and it wasn't important for the others either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if it would mean to give up your property and to permanently go to a third country; is that a correct understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on the whole, most of the detainees did that. They left and they went to third countries. The Red Cross was present there. People went to Karlovac, countries would be selected, certain countries would accept certain people, according to the agreement, and people would cross the ocean, for example, and go to these countries. And now that 11 years have passed, some people haven't returned to their country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Let me just try to stop you for a second. You're now describing what happened to those people. My question was that even if you would have read the document and even if that would have contained that you declare to give up your property and to leave your country permanently, and if that would have been the content, you would have been willing to sign.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regardless. Each of us would have signed, not only me, but others too. They would have signed whatever needed signing just to leave that hell-hole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Ms. Loukas, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Medanovic, you'll now be examined by Ms. Loukas, who's counsel for the Defence. Cross-examined by Ms. Loukas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Medanovic.

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Medanovic, I don't have many questions for you, but I just want to ask about your awareness or otherwise of certain events. Do we understand each other?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you everything I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you aware whether Mr. Omer Filipovic was in control of armed Muslims in Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Omer Filipovic was my professor at school, my teacher, and he was the presiding office [as interpreted] of the SDA party. Omer Filipovic was a sort of president. I knew about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Were you aware of him being in charge of armed Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew he was at the head of the Muslims, but not armed Muslims, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not aware of him being in charge of Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I -- or rather, while I was in Kljuc, I didn't see a single Green Beret. I don't know what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of Mr. Filipovic being in charge of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't aware of that. I knew that he was some sort of president of the SDA or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of, around the 27th of May, 1992, Green Berets blocking the regional road between Kljuc and Sanski Most in the town of Krasulje?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about the incident several days later, but I didn't know who it involved or what happened or what the purpose of the incident was. I didn't know anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of Mr. Stojkovic Dusan, the assistant commander of the police station in Kljuc, being killed around that time?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about that too, that it had taken place. I heard about it from others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you aware of any Muslim involvement in that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had heard about that. Of course they were involved in the incident, because at that period of time, as you said, the 27th of August, that was when there was a lot of unrest in town, and a Muslim, a Muslim man could not pass through Serbian territory. It was not allowed. And the Serb who was the deputy commander or komandir from Kljuc, he didn't allow people to go through the village of Krasulje. He wasn't allowed to go through the village of Krasulje, which was a purely Muslim village. So he was denied access and that's how the incident came about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you've indicated in your answer, as it recorded in the transcript, 27th of August. I take it what you're -- the date we're dealing with there, the month we're dealing with there, is the 27th of May; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: May, May, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you also -- were you aware of an attack by Muslims on a group of members of the JNA who were retreating from Croatia into Bosnia-Herzegovina in your local area, in the Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I never knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, I have a brief clarification that I'd like you to give me. You said that the men were wearing military police uniforms and that they were -- some of them were masked. And you said that they wore the masks because they were afraid that you might identify them, recognise them. So how did you arrive at that particular conclusion?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: That's just my opinion. I don't claim that what I thought was correct, but I assume that they wore masks to prevent them from being recognised. Why would you wear a mask if nobody is going to recognise you anyway? So I think that that was the reason they wore masks, because they were from neighbouring villages, people from neighbouring villages. I don't claim that they were, but they did wear masks to prevent themselves from being recognised. Why they wore the masks, I can't really say for sure. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But were they all wearing the military police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. The ones that escorted us, they were all wearing military police uniforms, yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] You also mentioned some reservists. Were they just called in for that particular occasion or were they there anyway? Had they been recruited anyway?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't explain that. It's there -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] You didn't know them. You didn't know these people; they were people you didn't know. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of the people I knew, I listed those people. I said in my statement who I recognised and who I did not. Now, who wore what and why they were wearing what they were wearing, I can't explain that to you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, you identified, for example, a man by the name of Sico, and you knew him. And he was wearing the same reservist uniform, was he?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: No. He was wearing the military police uniform. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] What were the reservists wearing? How were they dressed? And how were you able to make the distinction?

utterances.speaker: AZIM MEDANOVIC
utterances.text: The military police distinguished in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or the former Yugoslavia, by the fact that they wear a white belt with white bands, white holsters for their pistols and details of that nature. An ordinary soldier does not wear that kind of thing. So that's how we differentiated between the military police and the reservists, a regular soldier, rank-and-file soldier. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Medanovic, let me first ask the parties whether the questions put by Judge El Mahdi have raised any need for further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not from me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Medanovic, this, then, concludes your testimony in this court, since I have no further questions for you. The Chamber would like to thank you for coming the far way from your country. It did not remain unnoticed -- yes. I'm now saying far away, but that might not be correct. The Chamber did not remain unnoticed that the questions and your own answers confronted you with a period in your past which, without any doubt, is very emotional for you. Thank you very much. And even if your way back is not as long as I suggested before, thank you very much for coming. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to thank you too, and I was willing to come here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have 20 minutes remaining. One of the oral decisions that was prepared is ready to be read out, but if you would grant the Chamber another ten minutes, the second one might be as well, and we could spend the last ten minutes in reading out the two decisions. One is the decision on the certificate and the other one is the decision about the videolink. So the parties are invited to remain on standby and we hope to be back in ten minutes. --- Break taken at 1.27 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will deliver two oral decisions. They have been provided to the booth. Even with my latest handwriting in it, which might not be easy to follow, but at least then you are alert on when the printed text does not serve any more. I will first start the decision on cross-examination of the witness Biscevic through a videolink. This is a decision pursuant to Rule 71 bis of the Rules. I would point out that Rule 71 bis was added to the Rules on the 17th of November, 1999. The present decision addresses a motion by the Prosecution of the 16th of September, 2004, to which the Defence replied on the 30th of September. Rule 71 bis states that, and I quote: "The Trial Chamber may, in the interests of justice, order that testimony be received via videoconference link." According to the case-law of the Tribunal, testimony given via videolink is no less reliable than testimony given by the witness physically present in the courtroom.
